t: Pan-Slavism grew from Romantic nationalism after the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars, when Slavic scholars of history, philology and folklore encouraged a sense of shared identity and ancestry.
Slavic thinkers disagreed about its aim: Palacký sought Slavic autonomy inside the Habsburg monarchy, Štúr proposed union under Russia, and most Serbian intellectuals wanted a South Slavic state.
The Poles largely rejected it as serving Russian interests, and the Bolsheviks treated it as a reactionary idea of the Russian Empire, so the ideal faded after the First World War.
dyk: When František Palacký was asked in 1848 to declare for German national unity, he replied that if Austria had not long existed, it would be necessary in the interest of Europe and of humanity itself to create it.
ev: The Napoleonic Wars end, and the Pan-Slavism movement begins to grow rapidly
The First Pan-Slav Congress meets in Prague from 2 to 16 June and is broken up when the army bombards the city
The Slovak National Council petitions Emperor Franz Joseph I to recognise the Slovak nation within defined borders
The Association of Serbian Philology commemorates the death of Cyril a thousand years earlier
A Slavic Congress meets in Moscow, boycotted by the Poles
The Kingdom of Yugoslavia unites most South Slavic-speaking nations under the Karađorđević dynasty
The split between Tito and Stalin ends the proposals to bring Bulgaria into a Greater Yugoslavia

f.thinkers: Ján Kollár, a Slovak poet who saw the Slavs as one nation of four tribes; František Palacký, the Czech historian who presided over the 1848 congress; Pavel Jozef Šafárik, a Slovak philologist; Ľudovít Štúr, who turned towards Russia; Juraj Križanić, a 17th-century Croatian missionary counted among the first pan-Slavists; Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, who completed the Euro-Slavist programme
f.texts: Štúr’s Das Slawenthum und die Welt der Zukunft (Slavdom and the World of the Future), written in the early 1850s and first published in 1867 in a Russian translation; Masaryk’s New Europe: Slavic Viewpoint; the anthem Hey, Slavs
f.ideas: the unity of the Slavic peoples; a shared Slavic identity and ancestry drawn from history, philology and folklore; the Slavs as one nation of four tribes; Slavic autonomy within the Habsburg monarchy (Austroslavism); union under Russian leadership; a South Slavic nation of three faiths; Euro-Slavism within the European Union
f.today: Pan-Slavism has little public following; parties that include it in their programmes live on the fringe or, in Belarus and Russia, in a controlled opposition, and apart from cultural and heritage organisations no form of union among Slavic countries exists
